content.text: As cities grew rapidly in the late 1800s, the amount of steel needed to construct houses and businesses increased.

explanationText.text: The graph shows the production of steel increasing during the late 1800s.  As cities grew rapidly, they needed to construct taller buildings for housing and businesses to conserve space. So, the demand for steel went up, causing production to go up as well.

content.text: New technological developments in the mid-1800s allowed steel to be produced more cheaply and efficiently than before.

explanationText.text: The graph shows that the production of steel sharply increased during the late 1800s. This was partly because new technology allowed iron to be converted into steel more cheaply and efficiently than before. This meant that more steel could be made quickly.

explanationText.text: The graph does not show that demand for steel slowed during the 1890s.

content.text: Worker protests for better wages and safer working conditions caused many steel factories to shut down in the late 1800s.

explanationText.text: Steel factory shut downs would have caused a decrease in steel production. The graph indicates an increase in steel production during the late 1800s.

also became an important industry. John D. Rockefeller was a leading oil industrialist. Read the passage about Rockefeller. Then answer the question below.

When John D. Rockefeller first invested in an oil refinery in 1863, oil was not yet a major industry. But as new technology made drilling more efficient and new products increased consumer demand, Rockefeller's business grew. One key to Rockefeller's success was his development of a new business strategy called

. Horizontal integration is when a business buys as many of its competitors as possible to reduce competition. By the 1890s Rockefeller's company, Standard Oil, controlled 90 percent of the oil industry, including drilling, processing, marketing, and sales.

textContent.text: Rockefeller's use of horizontal integration was controversial. His supporters claimed that his dominance improved efficiency and lowered prices for consumers. Rockefeller's critics, however, claimed that he used unethical practices to build his influence. Rockefeller might temporarily lower prices to pressure a competitor out of business, only to purchase the competing firm and raise prices again, harming consumers.

Other people referred to leaders of corporations as "robber barons," claiming that they became wealthy by taking advantage of their workers and cheating their competitors.

also became an important industry. John D. Rockefeller was a leading oil industrialist. Read the passage about Rockefeller. Then answer the question below.

When John D. Rockefeller first invested in an oil refinery in 1863, oil was not yet a major industry. But as new technology made drilling more efficient and new products increased consumer demand, Rockefeller's business grew. One key to Rockefeller's success was his development of a new business strategy called

. Horizontal integration is when a business buys as many of its competitors as possible to reduce competition. By the 1890s Rockefeller's company, Standard Oil, controlled 90 percent of the oil industry, including drilling, processing, marketing, and sales.

textContent.text: Rockefeller's use of horizontal integration was controversial. His supporters claimed that his dominance improved efficiency and lowered prices for consumers. Rockefeller's critics, however, claimed that he used unethical practices to build his influence. Rockefeller might temporarily lower prices to pressure a competitor out of business, only to purchase the competing firm and raise prices again, harming consumers.

also became an important industry. John D. Rockefeller was a leading oil industrialist. Read the passage about Rockefeller. Then answer the question below.

When John D. Rockefeller first invested in an oil refinery in 1863, oil was not yet a major industry. But as new technology made drilling more efficient and new products increased consumer demand, Rockefeller's business grew. One key to Rockefeller's success was his development of a new business strategy called

. Horizontal integration is when a business buys as many of its competitors as possible to reduce competition. By the 1890s Rockefeller's company, Standard Oil, controlled 90 percent of the oil industry, including drilling, processing, marketing, and sales.

textContent.text: Rockefeller's use of horizontal integration was controversial. His supporters claimed that his dominance improved efficiency and lowered prices for consumers. Rockefeller's critics, however, claimed that he used unethical practices to build his influence. Rockefeller might temporarily lower prices to pressure a competitor out of business, only to purchase the competing firm and raise prices again, harming consumers.

pieces.text: The period from the 1870s to the early 1900s in the United States is known as the
. During the Gilded Age, working conditions changed tremendously. Read the passage about some of these changes. Then answer the question below.
The Gilded Age was a time of significant economic growth and

, meaning a shift toward manufacturing. Before the Gilded Age, most Americans worked on farms or in small workshops as independent craftspeople. This meant the average worker had some control over their schedule, tasks, and pace of work. As production shifted from independent workshops to factories, workers encountered a drastically different environment. In order to maximize profits, Gilded Age factory owners expected workers to follow strict schedules. Many worked ten to sixteen hours per day, six days per week, for low wages. Unlike the skilled craftsmen of the past, many Gilded Age workers performed repetitive tasks, making the average factory worker easily replaceable.

contents.text: Which of the following statements describe how labor changed during the Gilded Age? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Job security increased because factory work involved more specialized skills.

textContent.text: The hands of these men would be crisscrossed with cuts, until you could no longer pretend to count them or to trace them. They would have no nails, – they had worn them off pulling hides; their knuckles were swollen so that their fingers spread out like a fan. There were men who worked in the cooking rooms, in the midst of steam and sickening odors, by artificial light; in these rooms the germs of tuberculosis might live for two years, but the supply [of germs] was renewed every hour.

Some men slip on the frozen blood on the floors.

contents.text: During the Gilded Age, the number of women who worked outside of the home for wages increased. While entering the workforce provided new opportunities, women also faced particularly difficult conditions. Read the passage about conditions for women working during the Gilded Age. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Working outside the home exposed women to new ideas and created a sense of unity with other women in the workforce. These connections contributed to the growth of women-led reform movements, including the women's rights movement. Employment outside the home also provided more economic freedom, allowing women—especially unmarried or widowed women—to support themselves rather than relying on male relatives. Women were also able to push back against stereotypes about gender roles, including the idea that they did not belong in the workforce.

However, women also faced new challenges in the Gilded Age. Many women worked in factories, where dangerous machinery often caused injuries or even death. Despite these risks, women were generally paid less than men for the same work because of the general assumption that women were not the primary breadwinners in their household. Women were also often excluded from joining organizations that helped workers improve conditions and get higher wages.

. During the Gilded Age, working conditions changed tremendously. Read the passage about some of these changes. Then answer the question below.
The Gilded Age was a time of significant economic growth and

, meaning a shift toward manufacturing. Before the Gilded Age, most Americans worked on farms or in small workshops as independent craftspeople. This meant the average worker had some control over their schedule, tasks, and pace of work. As production shifted from independent workshops to factories, workers encountered a drastically different environment. In order to maximize profits, Gilded Age factory owners expected workers to follow strict schedules. Many worked ten to sixteen hours per day, six days per week, for low wages. Unlike the skilled craftsmen of the past, many Gilded Age workers performed repetitive tasks, making the average factory worker easily replaceable.

In 1905, journalist Upton Sinclair wrote
, a novel about the working conditions in meatpacking factories in Chicago. Read an excerpt from
. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: The hands of these men would be crisscrossed with cuts, until you could no longer pretend to count them or to trace them. They would have no nails, – they had worn them off pulling hides; their knuckles were swollen so that their fingers spread out like a fan. There were men who worked in the cooking rooms, in the midst of steam and sickening odors, by artificial light; in these rooms the germs of tuberculosis might live for two years, but the supply [of germs] was renewed every hour.

…The workrooms at the meatpacking plants are unheated and dangerous in the winter. Men often suffer frostbite, and in desperation, stick their frozen feet into the steaming carcasses of cattle when the bosses aren't looking. The steam is so thick in the butchering rooms that it creates an extremely dangerous environment where men may be stabbed in a cloud of hot steam, or suffer other injuries. Some men slip on the frozen blood on the floors.

meaning.text: removing animal skins as part of the butchering process
a deadly respiratory illness

contents.text: During the Gilded Age, the number of women who worked outside of the home for wages increased. While entering the workforce provided new opportunities, women also faced particularly difficult conditions. Read the passage about conditions for women working during the Gilded Age. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Working outside the home exposed women to new ideas and created a sense of unity with other women in the workforce. These connections contributed to the growth of women-led reform movements, including the women's rights movement. Employment outside the home also provided more economic freedom, allowing women—especially unmarried or widowed women—to support themselves rather than relying on male relatives. Women were also able to push back against stereotypes about gender roles, including the idea that they did not belong in the workforce.

However, women also faced new challenges in the Gilded Age. Many women worked in factories, where dangerous machinery often caused injuries or even death. Despite these risks, women were generally paid less than men for the same work because of the general assumption that women were not the primary breadwinners in their household. Women were also often excluded from joining organizations that helped workers improve conditions and get higher wages.

contents.text: Read the information and look at the photographs about life for Chinese immigrants in the United States in the 19th century. Then answer the question below.

content.text: Chinese workers made up the majority of the labor force for the Central Pacific Railroad during the construction of the transcontinental railroad in the 1860s. Although they worked the same jobs as their white counterparts, Chinese employees were paid around 30% less. This photo shows Chinese railroad workers during a snowstorm. Historians estimate that over 1,000 Chinese workers died during railroad construction in the West.

As demand for labor in mines and railroads declined in the 1880s and 1890s, Chinese immigrants found it increasingly difficult to find jobs. Many started their own small businesses, particularly laundries and restaurants, which had minimal start-up costs and faced less competition from white businesses. This photo shows a recreation of a Chinese laundry that operated in California's Yosemite National Park. The business served park visitors and washed linens for a nearby hotel.

Many white, native-born Americans blamed immigrants for the crisis, arguing that they were driving down wages and "stealing" jobs by accepting lower pay for the same work. This led to a wave of anti-immigrant sentiment in the 1870s and 1880s, including violence against Chinese-American communities.

As anti-Chinese sentiment grew, cities and states passed laws restricting where Chinese immigrants could live and work. Eventually, the federal government passed the
in 1882. This law imposed a complete ban on the immigration of most Chinese people for ten years and was the first federal law to restrict immigration based on a person's nationality.

Non-laborers who wish to travel to the United States must obtain a special permit from the Chinese government proving their identity and profession.
The ban does not apply to representatives of the Chinese government or their servants.

Chinese people already living in the United States may continue to live and work in the country. Those who wish to leave temporarily must register for a "certificate of return" from the U.S. government before departing.

Chinese immigrants who arrived between 1850 and 1884 settled on the West Coast, particularly in California.

contents.text: Read the information and look at the photographs about life for Chinese immigrants in the United States in the 19th century. Then follow the instructions below.

content.text: Chinese workers made up the majority of the labor force for the Central Pacific Railroad during the construction of the transcontinental railroad in the 1860s. Although they worked the same jobs as their white counterparts, Chinese employees were paid around 30% less. This photo shows Chinese railroad workers during a snowstorm. Historians estimate that over 1,000 Chinese workers died during railroad construction in the West.

As demand for labor in mines and railroads declined in the 1880s and 1890s, Chinese immigrants found it increasingly difficult to find jobs. Many started their own small businesses, particularly laundries and restaurants, which had minimal start-up costs and faced less competition from white businesses. This photo shows a recreation of a Chinese laundry that operated in California's Yosemite National Park. The business served park visitors and washed linens for a nearby hotel.

Until the late 19th century, the United States had an "open door" migration policy, under which the federal government did not restrict immigration. As anti-Chinese sentiment grew, cities and states passed laws restricting where Chinese immigrants could live and work. Eventually, the federal government passed the
in 1882. This law imposed a complete ban on the immigration of most Chinese people for ten years and was the first federal law to restrict immigration based on a person's nationality.

contents.text: Read the information and look at the photographs about life for Chinese immigrants in the United States in the 19th century. Then answer the question below.

content.text: Chinese workers made up the majority of the labor force for the Central Pacific Railroad during the construction of the transcontinental railroad in the 1860s. Although they worked the same jobs as their white counterparts, Chinese employees were paid around 30% less. This photo shows Chinese railroad workers during a snowstorm. Historians estimate that over 1,000 Chinese workers died during railroad construction in the West.

As demand for labor in mines and railroads declined in the 1880s and 1890s, Chinese immigrants found it increasingly difficult to find jobs. Many started their own small businesses, particularly laundries and restaurants, which had minimal start-up costs and faced less competition from white businesses. This photo shows a recreation of a Chinese laundry that operated in California's Yosemite National Park. The business served park visitors and washed linens for a nearby hotel.

contents.text: In 1873, a major economic depression hit the United States, lasting several years. Many white, native-born Americans blamed immigrants for the crisis, arguing that they were driving down wages and "stealing" jobs by accepting lower pay for the same work. This led to a wave of anti-immigrant sentiment in the 1870s and 1880s, including violence against Chinese-American communities.
Read the list describing some examples of anti-Chinese actions. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: : After a white police officer was killed during a shoot-out between rival Chinese groups, a mob of around 500 people attacked Los Angeles's small Chinatown. Eighteen Chinese people with no connection to the shoot-out were killed. Ten rioters were found guilty of manslaughter, but the convictions were overturned by all-white juries, and the rioters were released from prison.

: After a fight broke out between white and Chinese miners, a mob formed and attacked the Chinese section of town. Twenty-eight Chinese miners were killed, and the survivors were forced to flee to a nearby town after the mob set fire to their homes. Sixteen white miners were arrested but never faced charges.
: An armed anti-immigrant mob marched through the city's Chinatown and forced residents out of their homes and businesses. The mob then set fire to Chinatown to ensure no residents would return.

in 1882. This law imposed a complete ban on the immigration of most Chinese people for ten years and was the first federal law to restrict immigration based on a person's nationality.

contents.text: Read the information and look at the photographs about life for Chinese immigrants in the United States in the 19th century. Then follow the instructions below.

content.text: Chinese workers made up the majority of the labor force for the Central Pacific Railroad during the construction of the transcontinental railroad in the 1860s. Although they worked the same jobs as their white counterparts, Chinese employees were paid around 30% less. This photo shows Chinese railroad workers during a snowstorm. Historians estimate that over 1,000 Chinese workers died during railroad construction in the West.

As demand for labor in mines and railroads declined in the 1880s and 1890s, Chinese immigrants found it increasingly difficult to find jobs. Many started their own small businesses, particularly laundries and restaurants, which had minimal start-up costs and faced less competition from white businesses. This photo shows a recreation of a Chinese laundry that operated in California's Yosemite National Park. The business served park visitors and washed linens for a nearby hotel.

textContent.text: In 1890, Louisiana passed the Separate Train Car Act, which required train companies to provide separate cars with equal facilities for Black and white passengers. Homer Plessy, a mixed-race Black man, challenged the law by boarding a whites-only car in New Orleans. Plessy was arrested but challenged the law in court. His lawyers claimed that the law violated the Fourteenth Amendment, which prevented the states from depriving anyone of equal protection of the laws.

pieces.text: The Supreme Court reviewed the case and decided that the Louisiana Separate Train Car Act was constitutional. The Constitution, the Court argued, protected
and
equality between races, but it did not require states to protect or enforce

equality. As the Court wrote, "If one race be inferior to the other socially, the Constitution of the United States cannot put them upon the same plane." In other words, if African American people felt that they were treated as inferiors by being forced to use separate facilities, the government was not legally obligated to do anything about it.

As Reconstruction came to an end, Nast's views about African American people changed, reflecting larger changes in white Americans' attitude toward Black Americans. Look at the following images. textContent.text: In 1890, Louisiana passed the Separate Train Car Act, which required train companies to provide separate cars with equal facilities for Black and white passengers. Homer Plessy, a mixed-race Black man, challenged the law by boarding a whites-only car in New Orleans. Plessy was arrested but challenged the law in court. His lawyers claimed that the law violated the Fourteenth Amendment, which prevented the states from depriving anyone of equal protection of the laws.

pieces.text: The Supreme Court reviewed the case and decided that the Louisiana Separate Train Car Act was constitutional. The Constitution, the Court argued, protected
and
equality between races, but it did not require states to protect or enforce

equality. As the Court wrote, "If one race be inferior to the other socially, the Constitution of the United States cannot put them upon the same plane." In other words, if African American people felt that they were treated as inferiors by being forced to use separate facilities, the government was not legally obligated to do anything about it.

decision?

It gave legal clearance for state and local governments to pass segregation laws that created "separate but equal" public facilities.
